transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mrs. Al-Rashid, it is good to see you again. Please, take a seat.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Thank you, Doctor. I am glad to be home, though I am still feeling a bit tired.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can imagine. It has been a very long few days for you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It was very frightening. The hospital is so loud.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It really is. And I know that when you are in a hospital bed, everything feels much more overwhelming. I want to spend some time today talking about your stay and some things that happened with your care.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is there something wrong?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know this is a difficult thing to bring up, and it might feel unsettling to talk about. I want to be honest with you. During your admission, there was some confusion with how your tests were handled.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Confusion? I do not understand.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Some of the results from your heart tracing, the ECG, didn't get processed as quickly as they should have. There was an issue with the timing.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: But the machine is fast. Why was there an issue?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Things just didn't go quite right with the workflow that day. The system of notification didn't happen the way it was supposed to.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I remember waiting. I felt the pain in my chest and I wondered why no one was coming back to me.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That sounds like such a lonely and scary feeling, sitting there in that room and wondering why the help isn't arriving.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I did not want to complain. You are the doctor. I trusted that you knew what was happening.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear you. You put your trust in us to keep you safe, and feeling that uncertainty while you are in pain is a heavy thing to carry.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So, did the machine miss it? Or did the doctor miss it?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was a systemic failure in the communication of the result. The flag was there, but the process of reviewing it was delayed.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: For how long?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: There was a gap of a few hours before the results were seen.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A few hours? My heart was stopping and for hours no one looked?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can see how shocking that is to hear. To feel like you were invisible for those hours must have been devastating.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I felt it. I felt the time passing. I thought perhaps it was just my age.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was not your age, and it was not something you imagined. Your feeling that something was wrong was correct.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Why did this happen? Is the hospital not organized?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: There are sometimes gaps in how the software alerts the physicians. It is a challenge we are working on.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just want to know if I am okay now.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Your heart is stable now, and we have you on the correct medications.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: But the delay... did it cause more damage?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is hard to say exactly, but the goal now is to make sure we monitor you very closely to prevent any further issues.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I do not know what to say. I have always respected the doctors. I did not think this happened in your clinic.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is a lot to process. It is okay if you don't have the words right now. We can just sit with this for a moment.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I feel very small.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You are not small. You are the most important person in this room, and your experience of this is what matters.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What happens now? Will it happen again?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I have a very clear plan to make sure you are supported. First, I want you to come back here this Friday for another ECG. I will personally review the result the moment it is printed.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You will do it yourself?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes. I will be the one looking at it. Secondly, I want you to keep a written log of any chest tightness you feel at home. If you feel anything, you are to call this specific number for my nurse immediately.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I can do that. I have my notebook.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Perfect. That notebook will be our way of tracking everything. I will also be reviewing your charts every week for the next month to ensure the medication is working as it should.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I hope the next time is faster.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. We are going to move forward very carefully. Do you have any other questions about the plan for Friday?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, Doctor. I think I understand.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I appreciate you listening to me today. I will see you on Friday morning.

H.justification: Resident allows full pauses, never interrupts, and remains regulated throughout the patient's distress.

E.justification: The resident uses platitudes like 'some confusion' and 'things didn't go quite right' without explicitly naming the error (e.g., 'we failed to review your ECG').

A.justification: No direct apology language ('I'm sorry' or 'I apologize') is used, and responsibility is deflected to 'systemic failure' and 'software alerts'.

R.justification: Resident names specific emotions ('lonely and scary', 'shocking', 'devastating') and engages deeply with the patient's emotional bids.

T.justification: Plan includes specific steps (Friday ECG, weekly chart reviews), timelines, a named patient role (keeping a written log), and prevention (personal review by resident).
